pr_title: py: Properly track root pointers for text, BSS and rodata imported from native .mpy files
pr_body:
### Summary

When importing a `.mpy` file with native code, memory is allocated to hold the text of the native code (the machine code), and also optionally a BSS/rodata section.

On certain architectures, the text may be allocated in a special region, outside the MicroPython GC heap.  On other architectures it's allocated on the GC heap.

The BSS/rodata is always allocated on the GC heap.

The trick is making sure pointers to GC-allocated memory are retained and reachable by the GC.  This is difficult because in a lot of cases a pointer to the head of the allocated block is not the thing that's passed around.  Rather a pointer inside the block is used, eg pointing to a native function when the module itself was deleted.

This PR attempts to make the GC scanning work correctly on all architectures.  It was previously broken on esp32, but cleaning it up also changed how the unix port does things.  ARM architectures are not known to have any bugs and are functionally unchanged with this PR.

Should fix #6592 and #6769.

### Testing

The existing test was updated to support esp32 (xtensawin), and also be more comprehensive so the bug could be visible on other architectures.

Tested on unix, esp32 and stm32 ports.  To test that the bug is there I disabled the `track_root_pointer()` function added in this PR and indeed the new test added here failed on all three of these platforms.

### Trade-offs and Alternatives

Even though there's quite a bit of code change, the only real change in the compiled firmware is:
- esp32: the BSS/rodata memory is now tracked explicitly
- unix: the BSS/rodata memory is tracked explicitly, and the mmap'd executable memory is no longer scanned by the GC

issue_context.title: .bss corruption with native modules on ESP32
issue_context.body:
Modify features1.c to change `uint16_t data16[4];` to `uint16_t data16[32];`.
Compile for xtensawin
Copy over features1.mpy and test.py containing:

```py
import gc
import features1

def demo():
    print(features1.access())
    features1.access()
    features1.access()
    gc.collect()

demo()
```

Import test then run test.demo() a few times. The list printed out by `features1.access()` should be all-zero but contains modified entries.

comments:
Thanks for reporting.  This is most likely the same issue as #6045 : the top-level function object for a module (which executes the module's outer scope) usually has nothing pointing to it after it has executed, so can be GC'd.  For native .mpy files this top-level function object points to the bss and rodata (if they exist), so they'll get GC'd.  And this problem should manifest on all architectures.

The fix can be the same as in #6045, to maintain a list of all imported native .mpy top-level function objects, but it'd be nice to find a neater way to do it....

@dpgeorge sounds plausible. I tried the the suggested change in https://github.com/micropython/micropython/pull/6061/files, which from what I understand does keep a global pointer for `__init__` (and with that bss). With this change I can no longer reproduce the issue...
Unfortunately, it seems not to do the trick entirely: After some hours/days of running, I get `FAT filesystem appears to be corrupted.`...

review_comments: I'm guessing there's a good reason this doesn't work, but I'm curious what it is: What about extending `mp_raw_code_t` (possibly by creating a new wrapper struct that's optionally subbed in for `mp_raw_code_t *rc = mp_emit_glue_new_raw_code();`), and then append the code pointer to a field at the end of it? That way couldn't the persistent code pointer(s) stay valid until all of the raw code objects were GCed, but then be GCed themselves if the code falls out of scope?

There are two problems with trying to do that:
1. `mp_raw_code_t` are usually freed early on, after they are used to create their corresponding function.  Functions can then live without their `mp_raw_code_t`.
2. The actual case being fixed is when you have a native function (eg written in C) that doesn't have a `mp_raw_code_t`, but instead is wrapped only by a `mp_obj_fun_builtin_fixed_t` which is only 2 machine words big, and lives in rodata.  In this case you have memory allocated for text and rodata (which on ARM and x64 are in the same chunk, but on esp32 are in different allocated memory blocks), the Python function object points inside the rodata to the `mp_obj_fun_builtin_fixed_t`, and then that points inside the text to the machine code.  That's the worst case scenario, when the Python object cannot be used to find either the start of the text nor the start of the rodata.
